Mr. Speaker, my purpose in entering the debate at this time is this:	a few moments ago, not in
my hearing but in the hearing of hon. members in the house, the hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Bruneau) assumed, and stated -and from the evidence he had in his hand I do not blame him for so stating-that I had at a certain meeting, where I met certain members of trade unions in Saskatoon, namely on the night before I caught the train to come to Ottawa, made certain statements. His statement was that I am reported in the Star-Phoenix as having said that I was opposed to the freezing of wages and prices now.
The hon. member has been most friendly about it, and has shown me the clipping. While I have found that, generally speaking, the reporters serving my home-town paper, the Star-Phoenix of Saskatoon, are very accurate, this is one occasion where they made a most distinct error. I did notice at the meeting at which I spoke that the young lad who had been sent to report the meeting was just that. He was a young lad; and I did hope that, in the light of the somewhat technical manner in which I discussed the subject, he would get the facts straight.
Until today I had neglected to renew my usual request that the Star-Phoenix be supplied to me here. The result is that I have had no opportunity to see that newspaper. I could have seen it of course if I had gone down to the reading room; but I did not do so. The result is that its being brought to my attention by the hon. member for Prescott was the first intimation, with one exception, concerning the mistake that had been made. One

of the people who, of late, have been sending us cards in regard to price controls-and some of these are friends of mine-wrote to me telling me about this mistake in the Star-Phoenix. I have on my desk the copy of the letter in that regard.
Let me add that at that meeting were represented I believe every trade and industry in Saskatoon, including the two great labour congresses, the packing-house workers and others. People from nearly all the trade unions in Saskatoon were represented. There was not one of the thirty or so men who met me who had any doubt whatever as to where I stand in the matter of price controls.
I spoke for forty minutes at the meeting, and I spoke in favour of price controls-just as I had spoken to forty-two meetings in various parts of this country during the last month or two, and spoken in favour of price controls. Many of those meetings were in the maritime provinces. I think therefore that I am thoroughly on record as to where I stand in respect of the control of prices. I am in favour of price control-and now. What I have said ought to straighten the matter out, so far as the house is concerned.
Then, so far as the hon. member for Prescott and the Star-Phoenix are concerned, I shall have something further to say. I have the highest regard for the Star-Phoenix, as a good newspaper. May I say in all kindness to the hon. member for Prescott that I do not see how he could have sat in the house since he was elected, whatever the date may have been

a year or two ago, I believe- and have listened to me speak in debate, along with other members of the group with which I am associated, and then in all sincerity accuse me of ever having made a speech of this sort. That I cannot fathom.
I am prepared however to give him the benefit of the doubt. I will not say that someone in his own party supplied him with a juicy item which purported to show that I, who only today seconded the amendment of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) in favour of price controls, had within the last two weeks addressed a meeting of trade union members in Saskatoon at which I had opposed the same thing.
I believe, sir, that I have made myself clear. As a matter of fact, I have penned a letter to the Star-Phoenix over my own name protesting this quotation. Then, in case hon. members are curious as to what I did say, may I offer an explanation? I said-and I would ask hon. members to listen carefully; my Liberal friends opposite would perhaps like to quote it to me on some other occasion -that "if you at this moment combine"-and note the word "combine"-"wage and price 80709-12j
The Address-Mr. Knight controls, and put them both now into effect that, in the present disparity which exists, that would be unfair and unthinkable, and would make permanent the high scale of profits now being enjoyed."
As I have said, there was no doubt in the minds of all those trade unionists as to where I stood. We met there in a meeting held in favour of price controls, and I said to them what I have said to the house now.
I am sure now that the hon. member for Prescott will accept my assurance that I never at any time opposed price controls either in the house or out of it. Since I have become tantalized to the point where I have to make a speech, I shall proceed to put myself on record by giving some of the reasons why I believe price controls would be a good thing for this country, and why I think the lack of such controls bears heavily upon many people in Canada.
In the first place there is a demand for price controls from all parts of the country. I need not say here that the cost of living index has risen rapidly. Taking a base of 100 for 1939, we find that it has crept up to about the 170 mark. This simply means that anyone wishing to buy goods now must take $1.70 with which to purchase goods which would have cost $1 in 1939. That, may I say, is the figure for the general price index. That index covers commodities such as carpets, organs, electric refrigerators, and other items which are comparative luxuries for many people.
What is the price index for food? The last time I saw it the figure was 218. What does that mean to the people of Canada? What does it mean to the housewives? It means this, that when you or your wife go down town you must take $2.18 to buy that which formerly cost $1. One does not need a very large pocket in his overcoat to be able to carry home with him $2.18 worth of groceries.
That is what I have to say about price controls. It is not too bad for you and for me. It is not too bad for the man whose wages have been increased to a comparatively decent level; but it plays havoc with the old people in our country. How would you like to be living in a garret, as I saw people living in garrets in the slums of Saint John. I wish the hon. member from that city were here so that he could hear me say it. People were living there like rats-old people living up in third-storey garrets, with only $40 to spend in a month. Those people are not buying goods rated in the 170 price index; they are buying only one thing, food-and not too much of that.
After having seen those things, if I could come back here, stand in my place in the

The Address-Mr. Knowles house and say I was not in favour of price controls, under present conditions, then I would have, like many other members in this house must have, something pretty deadly on my conscience.
That is my stand on price controls. I could go on of course to deal in more detail with the matter. I did not know that I was going to make a speech when I came down here and found that the hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Bruneau) had made the statement he had. If there is any question in anyone's mind in regard to my attitude on this matter, that question has now been answered. I do not think I have a reputation for inconsistency in this house or outside. I say the things that I believe. I do not pussyfoot. I do not change my mind after a couple of weeks as the hon. member has suggested.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in support of the amendment that has been moved by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) and seconded by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) and to urge this house to vote for that amendment, asking as it does for the immediate reimposition of price controls. If some of my friends on the other side of the house feel that for some reason- merely because they feel they have to support the government-they cannot do so, I hope that all hon. members on this side of the house will support it and that there will be a few Liberals independent enough to express what I am sure they know are the views of the people of this country.
Before I go further into that may I say that inevitably a good deal of the discussion during this debate has been with reference to the international situation. That matter has been well covered by the leader of this group and by other hon. members so I do not need to elaborate further. I should simply like to say that in my view the Canadian people, now as always, can be counted on to measure up to any challenge with which they may be confronted, but I think it is also the case-and this is the point we have been trying to press upon the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and the government as a whole-that the Canadian people want their leaders to take every possible step, consistent with honour and basic principles, to avoid getting involved in war. If war comes, that is another story; the people of this country will meet that challenge if they have to; but first of all they want their leaders to do their best to avoid our getting into a general war, the extent of which could not but be catastrophic.


Other members of this group, including the hon. member for Saskatoon who has just resumed his seat, have endeavoured to impress upon the house and the government the seriousness of this problem of rising prices and inflation. Various answers have been given by the government as to why they are not prepared to embark upon a program of price controls. One of the reasons put forward is that to do so would put the government and the officials of various departments up against very difficult problems in connection with administration, enforcement and so on.
Let it be said right away that no one denies that there are difficulties involved in administering and enforcing a program of price controls. But we ask the government to set against the difficulties that they would have to deal with, and which are not insurmountable, the much greater difficulties that are facing the Canadian people from coast to coast. In almost every home in this country the problem of making both ends meet is becoming an impossible one, carrying with it a terrible sense of frustration. Surely the Canadian people have the right to expect their government and their parliament to take steps to help to alleviate that serious difficulty.
The argument that there are difficulties in the way comes with particular ill grace from the Canadian government in view of the proud boast that they have made, a boast they were justified in making, about the good job that they did in the field of price controls during world war II. I strongly urge that that argument be dropped and that the government face up to the problems confronting our people and bring in a program of price controls, and subsidies if necessary, with the least possible delay.
The hon. member for Saskatoon just referred to the fact that the cost of living index, which now stands at 172-5, is the over-all index and does not give the picture so far as individual items are concerned. He indicated that the last figure he had for the food index was 218. I telephoned the dominion bureau of statistics about two o'clock today to inquire as to the present food index and was told that the last figure they had was 220-2. In other words, the cost of food, already sky high, is still rising. We simply cannot get away from what this means in terms of difficulties and problems, in terms of lowered health and living standards for our Canadian people.
I had something to say during the session last fall about this, with particular reference to our old age pensioners. On that occasion I took some time in an attempt to turn the

The Address-Mr. Knowles
cost of living index as it was then into dollars in order to indicate the dollar value of the money we are now paying old age pensioners in terms of the 1935-39 dollar. I even prognosticated1 as to what might happen in the event of the cost of living index going over 170 by the time we got back here in January. 1 regret to say that my prediction was correct because the cost of living index has gone up past that mark and is still rising.
The result is that in terms of the over-all figure, let alone the special figure for food which is the most important one to our old age pensioners, the $40 maximum old age pension now being paid under federal legislation is worth only about $23 in terms of the 1935-39 dollar value. When you consider that the first Old Age Pensions Act provided a pension of $20 and that we are paying now only $23 in terms of the 1935-39 dollar value, surely it is time we did something for these despised and forgotten elder citizens of this country.
If you consider the food index of 220-2 and figure out how much of an old age pension is spent on food you will realize that we are probably giving our old age pensioners today less in the goods and services that they must purchase than was the case with the original pension. I want to say something more about this subject in a moment but at this juncture I simply refer to our old age pensioners as being one group who feel most stringently the effect of a rising cost of living, which seems to be in danger of continuing to rise until it gets completely out of sight.
The government tells us what other measures it proposes to rely on, such as its general fiscal policy. We are told that the government is going to wait and see what happens as a result of the controls being introduced in the United States. All these pronouncements are no help to our people. Pronouncements and theories do not help. What they want is the kind of legislation which this government demonstrated during the last war it could administer, and which it could bring in now to protect the health and living standards of our Canadian people.
I know that every once in a while when we press for price control someone raises the question of wage control. It has already been said in reply to that question, and correctly so, that we have a form of wage control right now. Remember that a great many workers of this country have their wages determined by collective bargaining. When a collective agreement is arrived at it must hold for a minimum of one year, and in some cases the term of the agreement is even longer. During that period of time wages are fixed, wages are
frozen, but prices continue to go up month by month putting our workers in an impossible position.
In fact I will draw it to your attention that this very House of Commons passed a wage freezing measure last fall when we were dealing with the railway strike. We passed a measure which fixed a ceiling beyond which the arbitrator of the railway dispute could not go. I should not say "we". Parliament passed it. I opposed it and so did all members of this group, but Bill 1 of last session fixed a ceiling of 7 cents beyond which the arbitrator could not go in adjusting the wages of the railway workers. It also fixed a floor of 4 cents below which he could not go, but that turned out to have no significance.
I wonder how many members of the house are aware of the fact that when Mr. Justice Kellock made his report and awarded 7 cents, for which the hon. member over here was expressing appreciation last night, he said in the report that if it had not been for the ceiling fixed by Bill 1 consideration would have had to be given to the possibility of awarding the workers 10 cents. Why did he say that? Because the agreement was to run for two years, and inevitably in that two-year period the increase in the cost of living would cut out the value of the increase that the arbitrator was awarding to them.
There is a case of a great band of workers who had their wages frozen by an act of parliament last fall for a two-year period, and yet we have members of the house unwilling to consider price controls to protect the standard of living given to those railway workers by the bill passed by this parliament, I submit the time has come when some members have got to get over just sticking to a position because that position is one that has been taken. We have got to face this matter and deal with it on its merits.
I am glad to note that our friends of the Progressive Conservative party are now supporting measures to combat inflation and the rising cost of living. I hope they will support our amendment which specifies one particular effective measure of doing that very thing. I cannot help but remember occasions in 1945, 1946 and 1947, during the parliament that was elected in 1945, when the government was getting rid of controls, we of this group were trying to have price controls retained, and our friends of the Progressive Conservative party were trying to get the government to get rid of controls even faster than the government was doing it. They have something on their conscience but I shall not berate them too much about it now. I am glad to see that they want parliament and the government
174	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Knowles to do something about the rising cost of living, and I hope there are a few Liberals at least who will also represent faithfully the views of their people back home.
Just in passing, because I have referred to the Kellock report, I want to say how disappointed I was that that award discriminated between the railway workers on the one hand and the hotel and water transport workers on the other hand. Some hon. members may recall that last fall, when that matter was under discussion, I tangled with the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) about it. I was not satisfied with the wording in the bill but the Prime Minister assured me and the house that it was the intention of the government and of parliament that no group of workers should be asked to accept any legislation that would discriminate between one group and another.
The workers thought that meant that any award would apply across the board to all those involved in the dispute, but when Mr. Justice Kellock, who has shown his readiness to deal most fairly with the whole situation, read the terms of the act he did not find it that way. He found it necessary to make a different award giving a lesser increase of only 4 cents an hour, a different term of contract, and other differences to the hotel and water transport workers, to their disadvantage. The other day when I asked the Prime Minister about this matter I was sorry that he passed the buck to parliament. After all, the bill that parliament passed last fall was the bill that the government brought in, and it was passed, so far as this phase of the matter was concerned, on the assurance given by the Prime Minister on the floor of the house.
The hotel and water transport workers are deeply disappointed that they were not given the same award given to other workers involved in the dispute. There again it was a case where this parliament, by a bill that was enacted here, actually took the step of freezing the wages of certain workers at a certain level. If we can do that, if members of the house apart from this group have it on their conscience, as they ought to, that they did that job of wage freezing, the time has come when they should support the move for price controls to protect the health and living standards of the Canadian people.
I turn now to another subject to which I have already made passing reference, namely, the question of implementing the report of last year's committee on old age security. I noted that when the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) spoke today he was not very hopeful that we would get such legislation this year. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. 

Laing) on the other side of the house seemed to be a little more optimistic. I dare to hope that we will get that legislation this year. In fact, we must. One of the reasons that I hope for it is because of the reception that the house and the government gave to our report when the committee brought it in last year. Another reason is because of the terrific pressure for such action throughout the country. Another reason why I think it may be coming this year is because surely the government realizes that if it delays much longer the $40 a month plan is not going to be acceptable, is not going to be good enough. As a matter of fact time has already run out when that report seems as satisfactory as it did last June.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The government is not delaying at all.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Another reason why I am
hopeful that we are going to get action this year is because of what the Prime Minister said to me on February 5 in reply to a question which I put to him on the orders of the day, as recorded in Hansard on page 72. I am sure the reason for my question was quite clear. The speech from the throne says that amendments to the constitution relating to old age pensions may require to be laid before us at this session of parliament if the provinces agree to those amendments. So far so good. Personally I am not convinced that a constitutional amendment is necessary for the plan we recommended last year but if the authorities think we have to have a constitutional amendment let us get it and get on with the job of bringing in the legislation.
What worried me about the speech from the throne was that it stopped there. It said that the necessary constitutional amendments might be presented at this session. Well, we can get the constitutional amendments and go on home, and still not have the plan. We need one further step after the constitutional amendments have been enacted; that is, that the legislation implementing last year's recommendations be brought in. So I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) this question, and I will read his reply as well:
In view of the apparent readiness of the provinces to agree to constitutional amendments in one form or another regarding old age pensions, will an effort be made, as soon as agreement has been obtained, to present those amendments to parliament in time so that legislation implementing last year's old age pensions recommendations may be enacted at this session?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I would not like to confirm or to detract from the apparent optimism of the hon. member with respect to the readiness of the provincial governments to agree to constitutional amendments which would enable that to be dealt with.

As stated in the speech from the throne, the matter is before the provincial governments for their consideration, and it is and will be the policy of the government to avoid any possible delay when agreement has been reached to have that agreement implemented.
When I suggested that there was apparent readiness on the part of the provinces to agree to these amendments, I did so because I had read the correspondence between the government and the provinces tabled in this house on February 1 and included in an appendix to Hansard. That correspondence reads pretty well; I do not think anyone could feel any discouragement from any of those letters. The worst you find is one or two premiers saying the matter will be studied and considered. But in addition to that correspondence a number of legislatures have been called into session and speeches from the throne have been read. In every instance it has been indicated that the provincial government concerned proposes to bring in legislation or resolutions asking the authority of the legislature to agree to the whole plan under consideration. Well, Mr. Speaker, the provincial legislatures will all conclude their sessions and prorogue long before this session is finished; in fact a number of them will be through a couple of months from now or sooner. That means that six weeks or two months from now there is every likelihood that we will know whether or not the provinces do agree to the plan and to any constitutional amendments which may be necessary, and I am hopeful that they will agree, and that we will know it soon. I now have the Prime Minister's word, as I read it from page 72 of Hansard, that if and when that agreement is indicated there will be no delay in having it implemented.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if at the end of March or early in April we know that the provinces agree, there will be plenty of time before this session ends to take both steps, that is, to amend the constitution and then bring in legislation implementing the old age pension plan recommended to parliament last year by the committee. I strongly urge, in the words of the Prime Minister, that there be no unnecessary delay. I hope the provinces and the public generally will continue to press for speed in this matter, and that this legislation will not be put off until just before the next election, but that we will get it into effect this year.
As the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) and other members of the committee know, just as soon as this plan is put into effect some of us will start a campaign to have it improved, That $40 is not enough. That means test from 65 to 69 should not be there. But at the moment our
The Address-Mr. Knowles job is to get that plan, which has unanimous support, into effect, and none of us should say anything to jeopardize the success of that effort. On the other hand I ask the government to act in good faith and see to it that these constitutional amendments are not unnecessarily delayed, which could have the effect of putting off this necessary legislation until next session. The time for the old age pension legislation itself is as soon as possible, certainly at this session of parliament.
On the orders of the day this afternoon I put another question to a minister, this time to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I must say that his answer was at least forthright and categorical, even though not satisfactory. I asked him whether the government would consider setting up at this session of parliament a special committee similar to the committee of last year on old age security, to study and report on the whole question of health insurance for the Canadian people. As I say, I was sorry the minister found it necessary to say it was not the intention of the government to set up such a committee this session. I think it is fair to say that at the end of the sittings of the committee last year those of us who were members were pretty well agreed that a committee such as I asked for today would be a good idea. I am free to confess that when it was first proposed to set up an old age security committee last session I criticized the proposal as a delaying move. Well, we still have not had the legislation, which we should have had last year, but at least I will say that the committee did a good job. We collected a great deal of material; we publicized that material, and members of the House of Commons and the public generally are better educated on the subject of old age pensions because that committee met. Also as a result of the work of that committee there is hope that we will get this better legislation this year and from there we can fight on for something better still.
During the course of our discussions in that committee we frequently moved over into the field of health and time and again we faced the fact that something needed to be done in that field as well. So I say that at the end of our sittings there was pretty general agreement, even if it was informal and off the record, that at another session it would be a good idea to have a similar committee which would make a similarly exhaustive and worth-while study of the question of health insurance for our Canadian people. I hope the international situation is not being used by the government as an excuse for not setting up such a committee.

The Address-Mr. Knowles As a matter of fact I see the international situation as a reason for taking steps of this kind. If we are heading into any kind of international difficulty it will be all the more necessary to integrate and rationalize our health and medical set-up in this country, and all the more necessary to give our people an assurance of security in the field of health as well as the field of old age pensions.
The other day I was pleased when the new hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan), in moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne, spoke from his own experience as a doctor and asked for health insurance because of the many cases he knew of where people had their life savings wiped out or their entire future mortgaged because of unexpected and heavy hospital or medical bills. This is something that really concerns a great many of our people and makes for a great deal of insecurity and unhappiness. This government and this parliament could do something about it, and I would hope that reconsideration will be given the proposal I put to the minister today in the form of a question, which unfortunately he answered in the negative. Let us at least have a committee, and get started at this important job.
There is just one other matter to which I should like to address a few remarks. Many of us were very disappointed with the announcement made the other day by the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters), when he indicated that the amount of the down payment on new houses under the National Housing Act was to be increased as from the day he made the announcement. We all know that in a time like this there are shortages and that because of those shortages, in steel products and other building materials, there may have to be some cutting back of building of one kind or another. But surely the course to follow is decide on the basis of what is needed, and first of all to decide as between business and recreational buildings and homes. Surely, when it comes to homes, the decision should be made as between high-priced homes and medium or lower priced homes which are needed by more of our people. Surely, some formula could have been worked out which would have conserved materials intelligently, and in such a way as to make materials available where they are most needed. But no; the government simply announces, through the Minister of Resources and Development, that it is going to attack this problem by increasing

the amount of the down payment, starting with the little fellow who can build a new house only if he can get a fairly substantial mortgage, particularly under today's high prices. Mr. Speaker, I do not like that kind of legislation. There is one word that fits it that members of this house do not like, but that is what it is. It is class legislation. It is not dealing with a serious problem in a reasonable and proper way, and I object most strenuously to it.
A day or so ago I happened to meet a friend of mine who is connected with the building of houses. It was just after that announcement, and I asked him what the effect would be. I went on to suggest to him that it might slow down the building of new homes. His reply was, "Slow it down? It will stop it altogether." The great mass of the people who need homes have to be able to raise a substantial mortgage in order to build a house at all. If that is the result, to cut back the building of homes at a time when rent controls are coming off, just look at the additional problems that will be thrown on the shoulders of our people. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that such actions do not coincide with the responsibility that the government of a country owes to its people.
It is true that our people are absorbed in the international problem. It is true the government is absorbed in that problem, and we would criticize them if they were not giving very close consideration to all that is involved in the world situation. But I strongly urge that they must not let their absorption with international affairs blind them to the necessity of dealing intelligently and fairly with problems at home. I most strongly urge that this house support the amendment which is now before it requesting the immediate reimposition of price controls. I urge that there be no delay in bringing in not only the constitutional amendments but legislation implementing at least the terms of last year's old age security plan. I urge reconsideration of the proposal for a committee on health insurance, and I hope that we will yet get a more intelligent way of dealing with shortages of building materials, because our people still need homes. Homes, health, and security are important all the time. It is particularly important that attention be paid to these things at this critical time in the history of our nation and our world.
On motion of Mr. Howe the debate was adjourned.
